title: SEAL: Scaling to Emphasize Attention for Long-Context Retrieval

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to identify why LLM long-context retrieval degrades and locate which model components are responsible, enabling targeted improvement. Paper [3] ("Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality") shares a substantively equivalent purpose. It investigates how specific attention heads are responsible for retrieval in long-context LLMs, aiming to understand and explain the mechanisms behind long-context retrieval. This aligns with the goal of identifying components responsible for retrieval degradation. No other paper explicitly addresses this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves head-wise and channel-wise pruning experiments on LongChat-7B-32K, combined with direct-effect circuit analysis, to reveal specific attention heads and channels that correlate with retrieval performance. Paper [7] ("On the Weak Link between Importance and Prunability of Attention Heads") conducts head-wise pruning experiments to analyze the role of attention heads in Transformer models, which is substantively equivalent to the pruning-based analysis in the contribution. Additionally, Paper [20] ("Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability") describes a systematic process for identifying neural network components involved in specific behaviors, which overlaps with the circuit analysis aspect of the contribution. Together, these papers cover the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses the LongEval line-retrieval benchmark on LongChat-7B-32K, measuring accuracy changes due to pruning and scaling of specific attention heads. Paper [3] evaluates retrieval performance by analyzing attention heads' roles in long-context factuality, which involves a similar evaluation design (head-level analysis of retrieval performance). Paper [7] also evaluates the impact of pruning attention heads on task performance, which matches the evaluation design of measuring performance changes due to head pruning. These prior works cover the evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is LLM interpretability and long-context retrieval. Paper [3] explicitly operates in the same domain, focusing on understanding the mechanisms behind long-context retrieval in LLMs. No other paper directly addresses this domain.

**PURPOSE: Identify why LLM long-context retrieval degrades and locate which model components are responsible, to enable targeted improvement.**

Paper [3] "Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality" directly pursues the same objective: "Our systematic investigation across a wide spectrum of models reveals that a special type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving information." This is the same purpose — identifying which model components are responsible for long-context retrieval behavior. Paper [20] pursues mechanistic interpretability localization more generally but not specifically for long-context retrieval degradation. Paper [3] is the closest match at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: Head-wise pruning experiments + channel-wise pruning + direct-effect circuit analysis to identify specific attention heads and channels responsible for retrieval.**

Paper [3] identifies retrieval heads via "systematic investigation" but uses attention pattern analysis (sparse attention patterns) rather than head-wise pruning experiments. Paper [7] "On the Weak Link between Importance and Prunability of Attention Heads" explicitly uses head-wise pruning to analyze attention head roles: "We analyse the importance of basing pruning strategies on the interpreted role of the attention heads." Paper [20] uses activation patching (causal tracing) for mechanistic interpretability localization, which is related to direct-effect circuit analysis. The combination of head-wise pruning + channel-wise pruning + direct-effect analysis as a unified mechanism for this specific purpose is not fully covered by any single paper. However, paper [7] covers head-wise pruning as the core primitive, and paper [20] covers circuit/activation-patching analysis. Paper [16] also covers activation patching methodology systematically. The mechanism is a combination, but the core primitives (head pruning for importance analysis, circuit analysis) appear in [7] and [20].

**EVALUATION: LongEval line retrieval benchmark on LongChat-7B-32K; pruning single heads changes accuracy by ~+/-20%; scaling heads improves accuracy.**

Paper [3] uses long-context retrieval tasks to evaluate attention head behavior. Paper [1] introduces LooGLE as a long-context benchmark. The LongEval line-retrieval benchmark is a specific named benchmark. No prior paper appears to use LongEval line-retrieval as the evaluation design for head-pruning experiments. The evaluation design here — pruning/scaling individual heads and measuring accuracy change on LongEval — is a specific protocol. However, the general design of "prune/ablate attention heads, measure task accuracy" appears in [7]. The specific benchmark (LongEval) combined with the head-scaling intervention is not found in prior papers. But per the special rule, the evaluation DESIGN (ablate heads, measure accuracy on a retrieval benchmark) is covered by [7]'s head pruning + accuracy measurement design.

**DOMAIN: LLM interpretability / long-context retrieval.**

Paper [3] works directly in LLM interpretability for long-context retrieval. Paper [20] works in transformer mechanistic interpretability. Both cover this domain area.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to improve LLM long-context retrieval cheaply without altering learned knowledge, by emphasizing retrieval-relevant attention.  
- **Paper [7]** ("Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality") investigates retrieval heads in long-context LLMs, focusing on their ability to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within a long context. This aligns with the purpose of improving retrieval-relevant attention for long-context tasks.  
- **Paper [9]** ("LongHeads: Multi-Head Attention is Secretly a Long Context Processor") addresses improving long-context processing efficiency by leveraging multi-head attention mechanisms, which overlaps with the goal of enhancing retrieval-relevant attention.  
Thus, the purpose is **COVERED** by these papers.

### Mechanism
The contribution mechanism is SEAL, a learning-based attention scaling method that fine-tunes learnable per-head scalars (SEAL-H) or per-channel vectors (SEAL-C) via SGD/AdamW for 1 epoch, using ~50 format-consistent zero-shot samples.  
- **Paper [1]** ("HiFi: High-Information Attention Heads Hold for Parameter-Efficient Model Adaptation") introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that leverages attention heads for adaptation, which is conceptually similar to SEAL's mechanism of scaling attention parameters.  
- **Paper [11]** ("Density Adaptive Attention is All You Need") proposes a probabilistic attention framework (DAAM) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, integrating learnable parameters into the attention mechanism. This overlaps with SEAL's approach of fine-tuning attention parameters.  
- **Paper [13]** ("A Rank Stabilization Scaling Factor for Fine-Tuning with LoRA") discusses scaling factors for fine-tuning with LoRA, which is a PEFT method similar to SEAL-L and SEAL-D.  
Thus, the mechanism is **COVERED** by these papers.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses LongEval line retrieval and Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmarks on LongChat/Vicuna/Mistral models, with metrics like retrieval accuracy and efficiency (<1 hour tuning, ~0.002% of parameters).  
- **Paper [17]** ("RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?") uses the Needle-in-a-Haystack test for evaluating long-context LLMs, which matches the evaluation design.  
- **Paper [16]** ("Summary of a Haystack") proposes a synthetic benchmark for long-context evaluation, which is conceptually similar to Needle-in-a-Haystack.  
- **Paper [21]** ("Multilingual Needle in a Haystack") applies the Needle-in-a-Haystack test in multilingual settings, further confirming the reuse of this evaluation design.  
Thus, the evaluation is **COVERED** by these papers.

### Domain
The domain is LLM long-context retrieval and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.  
- **Paper [5]** ("Scaling Down to Scale Up") provides a systematic overview of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for LLMs, covering the same general application area.  
- **Paper [7]** ("Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality") focuses on retrieval mechanisms in long-context LLMs, which aligns with the domain of long-context retrieval.  
- **Paper [9]** ("LongHeads: Multi-Head Attention is Secretly a Long Context Processor") addresses long-context processing in LLMs, which overlaps with the domain.  
Thus, the domain is **COVERED** by these papers.

**PURPOSE: Improve LLM long-context retrieval cheaply without altering learned knowledge, by emphasizing retrieval-relevant attention.**

Paper [7] ("Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality") identifies that specific attention heads are responsible for retrieval in long-context LLMs, but its purpose is to *explain* the mechanism, not to improve retrieval cheaply. Paper [9] ("LongHeads") aims to help LLMs process long contexts but does so by restricting attention windows, not by emphasizing retrieval-relevant attention via learned scalars. Paper [3] ("LongSkywork") extends context length via training recipes, which alters learned knowledge. Paper [1] ("HiFi") targets parameter-efficient adaptation for downstream tasks generally, not specifically long-context retrieval without altering knowledge. No prior paper has the specific purpose of cheaply improving long-context retrieval by scaling/emphasizing retrieval-relevant attention heads without modifying the core model weights.

---

**MECHANISM: Generate ~50 zero-shot format-consistent samples, then fine-tune learnable per-head scalars or per-channel vectors via SGD/AdamW for 1 epoch.**

Paper [1] ("HiFi") fine-tunes attention heads selectively for PEFT, but uses importance scores to select heads rather than learning per-head scalars. Paper [11] ("DAAM") introduces learnable parameters into attention mechanisms for PEFT across modalities, but uses probabilistic mean/variance rather than per-head/per-channel scalars. Paper [19] ("GaAN") uses a convolutional sub-network to weight attention heads, which is a related primitive (per-head weighting) but in graph networks, not LLMs, and not via the same training scheme. Paper [5] and [15] survey PEFT methods including LoRA/adapters but don't describe per-head scalar learning. The specific combination of: (a) generating ~50 zero-shot task-specific samples, (b) learning per-head scalars or per-channel vectors as the sole trainable parameters, (c) applied to long-context retrieval improvement — does not appear in any prior paper. The closest is [7] which identifies retrieval heads but doesn't propose scaling them as a training method.

---

**EVALUATION: LongEval line retrieval and Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmarks on LongChat/Vicuna/Mistral.**

Paper [17] ("RULER") uses Needle-in-a-Haystack as an evaluation design for long-context LLMs and critiques/extends it. Paper [21] ("Multilingual Needle in a Haystack") uses the NIAH test design. Papers [22], [23], [26] also use NIAH-style evaluation designs. The LongEval line retrieval benchmark is a named benchmark used in prior long-context evaluation work. Both NIAH and LongEval line retrieval are existing named benchmark families/designs applied here to different models — this is a change of instance (which models are tested), not a change of evaluation design.

---

**DOMAIN: LLM long-context retrieval / parameter-efficient fine-tuning.**

Paper [7] works on long-context LLM factuality/retrieval. Paper [3] works on long-context LLMs. Papers [1], [5], [11], [13], [15] work on parameter-efficient fine-tuning of LLMs. Both sub-areas (long-context LLMs and PEFT) are clearly covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate that SEAL generalizes out-of-domain and composes with training-free context extension techniques without harming general ability. No prior paper explicitly establishes this empirical relationship. While many papers address long-context scaling (e.g., [3], [5], [6], [8], [19]), none report or establish the same relationship between SEAL's generalization, its compatibility with training-free extensions, and its preservation of general ability. This specific empirical finding is uncovered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves applying line-retrieval-learned scales to LongBench document-QA (out-of-domain) and measuring MMLU, as well as combining SEAL with NTK and Self-Extend context-extension techniques on Llama-2-7B-Chat. Papers like [6] (Self-Extend) and [8] (Dual Chunk Attention) describe training-free context extension techniques, and [3], [5], [11], [12], [17], [22], and [24] discuss various methods for long-context scaling. However, none combine SEAL with NTK and Self-Extend or apply line-retrieval-learned scales in the same way. The mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring MMLU performance (baseline/SEAL-H/SEAL-C = 42.53/42.34/42.17), maintaining or improving LongBench QA performance, and combining SEAL with NTK/Self-Extend to achieve dramatic retrieval improvements beyond the original 4K window at <1% of tuning costs. Papers like [3], [5], [6], [8], [11], [12], [15], and [19] use similar evaluation designs, including MMLU, LongBench, and retrieval metrics. The evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM long-context retrieval and generalization. Many prior papers ([3], [5], [6], [8], [11], [12], [17], [19], [22], [24]) operate in this application area, addressing long-context scaling, retrieval, and generalization. The domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Show SEAL generalizes out-of-domain and composes with training-free context extension without harming general ability.**

The purpose is to demonstrate generalization of a learned attention-scaling method (SEAL) to out-of-domain tasks and its composability with training-free context extension methods, while preserving general capability. Papers [6] (Self-Extend), [8] (DCA), [19] (XL3M), and [20] (InfLLM) all pursue training-free context extension, but none specifically pursue the objective of showing that a *separately learned* scaling method generalizes out-of-domain AND composes with other extension methods without harming general ability. The closest is [6] which shows Self-Extend preserves general ability, but the purpose here is specifically about SEAL's generalization and composability — a different objective (demonstrating a specific method's cross-domain transfer and plug-in compatibility). No prior paper covers this exact purpose at the problem-class level.

**MECHANISM: Apply line-retrieval-learned scales to LongBench document-QA (out-of-domain) and measure MMLU; combine SEAL with NTK and Self-Extend on Llama-2-7B-Chat.**

The mechanism involves: (1) transferring learned attention scales from one task to another (out-of-domain transfer), and (2) composing attention-scale modifications with NTK-based RoPE scaling [13,17] and Self-Extend [6]. Paper [6] introduces Self-Extend as a composable training-free method. Papers [13] and [17] introduce NTK-based scaling. However, the specific primitive of "apply learned attention scales cross-domain and stack them with other positional encoding modifications" is not present in any prior paper. No prior paper uses this combination primitive.

**EVALUATION: MMLU nearly unchanged; out-of-domain LongBench QA maintained; combined with NTK/Self-Extend improves retrieval beyond 4K window at <1% cost of tuning.**

MMLU as a general-capability preservation check appears in [3] ("extensive evaluation using language modeling, synthetic context probing tasks, and a wide range of downstream benchmarks"), [6] (Self-Extend evaluates on standard benchmarks to show no degradation), [17] (YaRN evaluates on standard benchmarks), and [11] (PI evaluates on tasks within original context). LongBench as an evaluation benchmark is used in [7] and implicitly in several long-context papers. The design of "measure general capability via MMLU + measure long-context task performance + combine with another method and measure" follows the same evaluation design pattern used in [6], [8], [17], and [3]. This is a standard evaluation design (benchmark family + capability preservation check) covered by prior work.

**DOMAIN: LLM long-context retrieval / generalization.**

Multiple prior papers operate in the domain of LLM long-context processing and generalization: [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [11], [12], [13], [14], [17], [18], [19], [20], [22], [24]. This domain is thoroughly covered.
